title: 7 Factors 3 Energy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares their personal experience of meeting strong aversion and doubt with mindfulness and discernment, allowing them to pass through without becoming stuck. They also explore how "sloth" or dullness can be met with energy, suggesting a shift in understanding of what it means to cultivate persistence and effort in Zen practice. Ultimately, Nomon emphasizes the importance of being present, letting go of effort and striving, and cultivating mindfulness through daily practice as an object of investigation into its nature and conditions.

The fifth one is doubt—doubt, like, "oh gosh," you know, that has many forms, right?
Always very compelling, very believable, doubt.

So I think the suggestion I made was to notice if any of these aversions arise, or which one seemed like most interesting or most powerful for you, and to see if we can meet them with the first two factors: meet them with mindfulness and discernment, with mindfulness and investigation, and sort of see if we can see a little more of what's going on.
That we're going to, like, solve everything or repair the machine like the machine is broken, which is to investigate in a certain way our experience.
So I'm kind of curious, did anybody do that?
Any observations you care to share with the Great Assembly?

Your little drama.
Yeah, it expands itself the next day, fine.
You know, it's not like the thing that I don't remember; it's just that it's no longer having control of me.

Yeah, and it really felt very different the next day.
Yeah, there's a way that the mind wants to make things sort of permanent, right?

So yeah, aversion and doubt and mindfulness of sort of strong emotion and just kind of go, "well, there's some factors of enlightenment."

After the first talk, you asked us to be aware of dullness.

Did everybody hear about that?

Yeah, I think so.

Yeah.

There was more going on inside.
So it didn't overwhelm me.
So the dullness was there and it was powerful through a wide focus.
Yeah, what we think of is sometimes these things, I mean, they get called hindrances, right, or dysfunction or dysregulation.
There are always negative pejorative terms for these different states, right?
But sometimes they might be really helpful.
They might be just the right thing to do, and the body just takes charge.
So maybe it is just absolutely skillful and helpful thing to be sort of dulled down or upset.
Definitely felt like the body.
Yeah, I learned something about this from a cognitive psychologist once.
He said, yeah, when you are working with people you have strong trauma and stuff, sometimes it is a really skillful response to just space out.
That is what they need.
Don't go telling them you have to experience your trauma all the time.

That becomes a habit and then it is not so good.
So I think that is another thing to look at when we hear these different teachings about it: is it better to be awakened than hindranced?

The question of not getting stuck there or identifying with it too much.
But you didn't.
You didn't identify with it too much, right?
And that would have been just all this sort of anger and roiled up feelings.

Happy Thanksgiving Eve.

So a lot of what we are talking about was energy, and that is the third factor of awakening is energy.

What kind of effort should we make?
What is skillful effort?

Science, experience, maybe there's somebody who doesn't agree with us, somebody in the couch potato culture, but maybe pretty much all agree that it would help us to have regular exercise and yet we don't always exercise regularly.

So just sort of casting our mind to that feeling of like, "I don't want to.
I'm tired.
I'll just lie here."
And that's a kind of a dullness, and a dullness in sort of the full sense of the word.
The hindrance that I translated dullness they originally translated as sloth and torpor.
So sloth and torpor.
So how do we meet sloth and torpor with energy?
And we've all had these occasions where it kind of could have gone either way.
We're tired, we don't feel like engaging, we don't feel like exercising, going on a jog, a walk, whatever it is for us, the gym.
And sometimes we don't make it and sometimes we do make it.
In my experience it's been the times that I make it I always end up with more energy.
With more energy.

We say, "I have energy or I don't have energy."
We tend to think of it like a gas tank, I think, don't we?
Like you sort of fuel up by sleeping and eating and whatever, renewing things kind of fuel you up and then you kind of use up your gas throughout the day and then you're out of gas.
Or we say that, "I'm out of gas."
And yet this experience of being tired and then exercising and having more energy doesn't fit that model, right?
Like why would more gas just appear in the tank because you drove faster, you know?
That doesn't fit that model.
So it's good to notice that we have these models that are not really accurate, you know?
They're not really true around energy.
Which is not to say that the opposite is true either.
The only thing we need to do is run faster, work harder, be more frenetic and then we'll always have more energy, right?
That's just a recipe for mania.
So that's not exactly true either.
So all of this stuff is a sort of experiential process like investigating, like, "what is it with energy with me?
How does it actually work?"
And not just sort of sad, not being satisfied with that sort of habitual voice in our head.
And then we have the question of energy in practice.
Like we know that it takes effort, right?
It takes energy to get here.
We got here tonight somehow.

And is it the same sort of quality?
Do we need a big push to get there?

And so that's an interesting thing to experiment with in Zazen.
So that's why I brought that up during the beginning of Zazen.
Because Zazen gives you a tremendous amount of feedback.
If you try too hard, it hurts, right?
You get feedback.
If you're not trying hard enough or not bringing up enough energy, it's dull, it's sleepy, it's spacey.
You're kind of weaving around in a daze.
And that's a simplistic sort of one-dimensional.
It has lots of different twists and turns.
And sometimes you're putting out what seems to be like an extreme amount of energy and you're falling right asleep.
And it's more subtle.
But Zazen kind of gives you some interesting feedback.
And so it's an interesting thing to sort of look at: what kind of energy is called for here?
And what's interesting when you hear teachings about the kind of effort that we should put into our practice is that they seem to come in sort of two categories: super effort and super letting go.
Have you noticed that?
So which one is it?
So I looked up and brought my favorite one of my favorite Zazen teachings on the sort of super going for it, super energy.
This is the introduction from the Gateless Gate koan collection by Wu Man, who collected this collection in the eleventh century.
And in his comment, he seemed to be all about just going for it.
So he's speaking about working with the koan Mu, the first koan in the Gateless Gate collection.
But you can just substitute practice in general when he says Mu.
So there's a sense where it's really beneficial to go for.
That's part of our Zazen tradition, you know, and an important part.
He said, *To realize Zan, one has to pass through the barrier set up by the ancestors.
Do not think that this barrier is the book.
It is right here in front of your nose.
Enlightenment is certain when the road to thinking finally stops.

If you are not an independent person, you do not pass through this barrier.
You cannot walk freely through heaven and earth.*
You may ask why these barriers are needed, or why the ancestors set them up.
This one word, Mu, is the barrier of Zan.
If you pass through it, you will see Zhaozhou face to face, and then you can walk hand in hand with the whole line of patriarch's.
Is it not a wondrous thing?
If you want to pass this barrier, you must work so that every bone in your body, every pore of your skin, is filled through and through with the question, "What is Mu?"
You must carry this day and night.

If you really want to pass this barrier, you should feel as though, this is the famous part, you should feel as though you have a red hot iron ball in your throat that you can neither swallow nor spit out.
Don't be afraid of this hot iron ball in your throat.
This means you can let go, you can be free.
And when your previous conceptualizing finally disappears, it is like a fruit ripening in season.
Subjectivity and objectivity are experienced as one.
And he goes on about how wonderful that is.
I thought you would like to enjoy that famous comment by Wu Man about the hot iron ball in your throat.
So there is this thread in Zen of like, you got to go for it.
Do not move.
Do not move, no matter how much your legs hurt, follow the schedule, right?
Show up, and you learn something from that.

Of course, we all need to modify the schedule, all that is included in this, but there is something that we learn from just dropping deeply into full commitment, commitment and enthusiasm for the way.
Because it helps us get over some of our sort of self-created limitations, right?
"I can't do that."
Oh yeah?
Let's see.
Let's check it out.
So it is a kind of investigation.
It sounds like machismo, so that is where we can run straight.
It sounds like just machismo and aggression, and we do it wrong, it can be that way.

Being in this body, in this practice, exactly the way I receive the instructions.
That is what I am going to do.
I am not going to modify it to suit my preferences and so on.

Like later?
After we have kind of dealt with a few issues, personal issues, then later we are going to wake up?
When is later?
So really giving ourselves to practice.

There is something to the other side as well.

Practice harder.
Be very present.
Stay with that breathing.
Be in that still body.
Bring up your energy, and then take a big breath and let go.

How much time?

Marvelous.

It's popping up.

And then the one last thought, and then we'll close, is in the realm of formal practice, I think a really interesting thing for us all to work on this week, this next week and forever probably, is the energy of daily practice at home.
The energy of daily practice at home.
What does it take to arrange our life, our attitude, our schedule, our what?
Bring up our energy so that we can have that wonderful experience, and it is a really wonderful experience of consistent practice at home, day after day.
That sort of weaving into our life of our home practice.

So to look at that, and not to look at it as something that we're just going to have to try harder, but to look at it as a sort of like an object of investigation to bring forward all of these tools and factors.
Like, what is mindfulness at play when I'm turning the alarm off and deciding whether or not I really want to get up now if it's a morning practice for you?

Where is discernment when I'm sort of making different choices about how I'm living and what are the causes and conditions that lead to ending up sitting or ending up not sitting, or whatever your home practice might be?
So it's not just a matter of "I should just try harder.
If I was a better person," that's not what we're talking about at all.
Because the Buddha said you're not a person anyway.
Forget about that being a better person thing.
This is about factors and causes and conditions and a sort of flow and a process and the way different things are supporting different things and causing things to arise or not arise.
It's like interference patterns.
So I suggest that as an inquiry for us for this next week, and maybe we'll talk about it a little bit next week, "Should we all be here?
What is the energy pattern and the attitude and the discernment and what are we aware of?
What's the mindfulness practice of trying to get ourselves to the cushion every day?
Maybe take one day off in a week, but not more than one.
We'll see how that is.
If you don't want to do that, that's okay.
But I think it could be really interesting.
And if you are somehow, lately, successfully making it to the cushion every day to still have this inquiry, not like, "Oh, good, I made it already.
Accomplished," to be curious.
Like, "Well, how did that happen?
How did I get here?
You sit down, how did I get here?
What is the feeling of this?
What were the causes that supported this?"
Because the other thing to realize that frees us up a little bit is it's not just our willpower ever.
Our willpower and our desire and our aspiration and our complicated whatever is always a part of it, but many, many more conditions far beyond, far beyond are coming together in each moment.

It might be, "You know what?

It might have to do with this, but causes and conditions are such that daily practice is not in the cards for me at this point."

That's what I do.
